blocks.x: Okay, well, Karen, if you just heard from Simon.

Alright. Well, he entered the hospital about six o'clock in the morning. I think it was Sunday morning, December 15th. And at that time we both walked in together. It was a very cold, windy, rainy day. Evening, night, all night it had rained. And he hadn't wanted to go to the hospital, but he was complaining of a sore throat. And his asthma attacks were coming on pretty rapidly during the night. So I thought it best if I just called the doctor at the time I was bringing him in. And his doctor had been out of town, but fortunately the doctor's brother was in town, who is a heart specialist. He told me to bring him right in. What was his name? Dr. Hyman. Dr. Edward Hyman was his physician, but Albert Hyman was the brother who admitted him. And not knowing of his condition, somehow together we worked out what he should have emergency treatment. And he was immediately put into the hospital room. We got a room for him with nasal oxygen. And we found that the nasal oxygen was not doing what it should have been doing, so we put him in a tent. And at that time, knowing of his blood deficiency, he had a blood count, which had rapidly gone up over the past few months prior to his entering his past last visit at the hospital. It had gone up to normal, and I was kind of worried. And I asked the doctor, he had put him on medications which she was allergic to, which would thin his blood out again, and cause his blood count to go down. And he said at that time, we were trying to prevent pneumonia. He noticed that the x-rays came back, they were clear. His heart did to the cardiogram, it was favorable. And he thought possibly just a few days in the hospital would put him back on his feet. In the meantime, apparently this virus that was going around, I forget the name offhand, the Hong Kong flu, they classified it as a Hong Kong flu. And his doctor came in, and he was getting along fairly, fairly well. His appetite was going. He had been eating very, very well in the past nine months prior to his death. He couldn't get enough to eat. He could get up in the morning, and the first thing he would say would be, what are we going to eat today? And he would be prepared for three, four full meals. And his weight stayed. He would gain a few pounds. He hit 104, 105 a couple times. And then the edema set in from the heart condition. And we went up to 106 pounds, seven pounds. And after he entered the hospital, his appetite started failing, failing very, very quickly. In fact, it started, he worked on a Friday evening, and on Saturday afternoon, I gave him his supper. And he kind of picked on it, which is unusual for him. He said we'd eat it later, and he started getting drowsy. And they put him on a very, on a salt-free diet at the hospital. His own doctor was not in, and naturally being in a heart specialist, a heart specialist had put him on a salt-free diet. Anybody that's eaten salt-free food knows what it tastes like. So he just wouldn't eat. And eventually, before we knew it, he wouldn't eat at all. I mean, he just stopped eating. So I asked Dr. Edward Hartman whether we could put him on at least on a low-sodium diet, where he would be able to have some taste to his food. And he put him on it, it was about two days prior to his death, he put him on this low-sodium diet. But I do remember in the hospital, sneaking him a couple pieces of pie, when he wanted it at night. He would crave for something sweet, and I'd go down across the street, and go to the restaurant, and I'd get him a nice, big piece of apple pie, and he'd gulp it down. That's about all the solid food he'd had, hoping the doctor wouldn't find out about the sodium and the salt in it. And he was very, very talkative in the hospital, his first few, first ten days he was in the hospital. And he was on continuous IV. They kept...
Let me ask you for some of the things that he was talking about and saying.

Well, he spoke of his past. We had in the past year, though, spoke much about his past, his life. He had mentioned... He pleaded with me not to take him to the hospital. He felt it would be his last trip in. And I told him I wouldn't never take him under his consent, other than he would be out. Like, I had taken him in September, even when he had a heart attack. He was unconscious for hours, is when I had taken him into the hospital, where he didn't remember going into the hospital. But this time he went in voluntarily, because he knew how worried I had been. And he just continuously kept trying to tell me of the future, of what should be done in case of his death. He had a premonition of it. And Christmas was coming upon him very rapidly. And he was anxious to get home, but he felt he wouldn't be home. I mean, his first words were, I'm not coming home for Christmas. And this is two weeks prior to, before Christmas had started, before I took him in almost, two weeks. And he had a feeling that he would not come home. And he would just talk of the grandchildren to be sure. I took care of his grandchildren and to be sure I was with Shirley, not to let her down, to stand by her. And this would be always haunted to me. And, uh, of his music. He would speak of his music. That, um, anything I can do to further it, in any way I should just continue it. That, that was his love. And he felt like that Friday when he shouldn't have gone in, that I was told him not to go in that last time he played. He was happy that I let him go in because he let him, he asked me whether he should. And I told him the best thing for him to decide would be for him. If he felt, I know he had felt worse many, many times for him to, uh, to go and play. If anything were to happen. That's the way he wanted to go, he always said. And there's many nights I sat there thinking it would be the night. But, uh, he would, uh, talk, he said he wanted, what he wanted played at his funeral. And to be sure that he would have, especially, uh, the composition of Over the Cross played. If I had to put on a phonograph. He said, have that played as he was leaving the church. And, uh, he told me not to, uh, worry too much. He said to hold my head up high. It would be hard. And, uh, continue in the manner I had been going. Oh, he spoke of the food. He says to try to remember how he had cooked so I would continue it. I don't know. He was just trying to establish me for the future without him. And naturally no one else accepted at the time. I listened and I just had heard it before many times when I took him into the hospital. But as the end was approaching, we prayed a lot. He's very, very spiritual anyway. He's a very religious man. And, uh, we prayed at home a lot, but we prayed much more so at the hospital. Uh, we prayed on the rosary beads. And he was, uh, asking me to read certain passages from the Bible. He was a big advocate of St. Joseph and St. Teresa. And, uh, he told me that when the time would come I would know when to bring his crucifix, his mother's crucifix, which was at home. He showed me where it was at the house. And he says, when it's near my time, you want to know. He said, bring me my crucifix. I want to go with my mother's crucifix. He had two. One that was on his mother's casket when she was buried. And one that his mother had when she held, when she died. So that afternoon before his death, I came home. I knew which one.
What was the afternoon before he died?

The afternoon. I came home. I hadn't been home for three or four days. I came home to take a shower because I had never left the hospital. I wouldn't come home for three or four hours and take a shower fresh enough and go back. And that afternoon, um, he couldn't talk. I let him know I was coming home to take a shower. And I sensed something was happening. The nurse had said he was doing fine. The doctor had tried to reassure me he was doing fine. And, uh, I came home and the first thing I asked Shirley, I said, Shirley, I'm taking your daddy's crucifix in this afternoon. And she looked at me and I said, uh, I don't want to, but I have to take it in this afternoon. So I took it in. In fact, I forgot. And I went halfway, I was by the bridge, turned around and came back for it. And his rosary beads, I always had his rosary beads that his mother had. I took them with me when I went into the hospital. I always took them with me. I grabbed his rosary beads as we entered into the hospital. So he always had his mother's rosary beads with him. But the crucifix, I did not give it to him until about 11, in the evening when I felt something was happening. And, uh, at that time I can sense his, uh, his mannerism was changing from manhood to childhood. His entire, his vision on his face was not of George Lewis the man. It was George Lewis the child, a child of God more or less. And, uh, I called the doctor and I asked the nurses to call him. And, uh, they called. And we worked on him pretty rapidly after that. But I put the crucifixion in his hand at 11 o'clock at night. He died at 2.15. And, uh, prior to that, uh, his last words that he spoke to me, that I can remember, he knew I was frightened. He told me he would never die in my presence. Which he did because he died in my arms. He said he would never do that to me. But he said he would never die. He never wanted to frighten me and die at home where I would have that fear of being completely left alone. Um, he said to me, he says, Carol, he said, Carol, I don't want to leave you. He said, but child, he says, I'll come back. I'll come back after you. He said, before things get too hard, he says, I'll be back after you. And they were the last words he ever spoke. Because after that we put the nasal, we put the tube down his nose. And it obstructed his throat and she couldn't speak. And he would motion to me by the wing of his nostrils, wiggling his nose. And, uh, in the hospital, he spoke of, uh, mainly, mainly Shirley and the grandchildren. And of his other children, he mentioned of them, he said to, uh, I probably would see him if he did pass away. In fact, every time I'd be whispering to somebody, he'd always come out of the way to talk about my funeral. He said, whatever you do, he says, but, he says, if you are, he said, be happy. He said, I don't want any sadness at my funeral. He said, I want a lot of music, the old rugged cross. I would like to be passed through the church, if possible. And, um, oh. What does he mean by that, passed through the church? Well, being that he was a Mason, he knew he could not be buried with a Catholic mass. Yeah. So he said, if I can get him at least into a church. Oh, I see. For some type of service. Yeah, right. Which he did. Which he did. We made it possible we had a service. And then he also had the Masons. And, um, oh, most of it that he spoke, it's hard to recall everything because he, uh, it was just as if he was home. I mean, what he would do in January, we were thinking in terms of what he would do when he first came home. He was planning to go back on tour. And, uh, his wish was to go back to Japan. Once, at least.
Good evening. Good evening.

And, uh, he's, he's, he's, he's mainly spoke of Japan. He also spoke of what we should do with his, uh, clothing if he did pass away. We shouldn't rush into anything too, too quickly. He said it would be a while before we would adjust to his absence. And, uh, to be sure. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening. Good evening.
We just weren't too hasty. And since then, we haven't been. We just had things as they are.
Can you remember some of the other people that came to see him at that time in the hospital?

Well, Mrs. Tate flew in from California. She wrote the book, Call on George, Dorothy Tate. He had very few visitors simply because he had been so ill that we weren't allowing many visitors. Bill Russell came to see him quite frequently, bless yourself.
Did George say anything about Bill Russell?

He said he's a living saint, always. And that's one person that whenever he came, George was asleep. If I had given him a shot for pain or for sleep, I always woke him up for that because I knew he wanted Issybill. Always. Even if it was just to look at him. Louie Nelson came in to see him. All of his sons came. No, all but one son came to see him. His two sons, by a former marriage, had come to see him. His daughter had not arrived, nor had his first wife arrived. The letter came, the second wife. And a few friends that had come in to the hospital to see other patients that had heard that he was in the hospital. I also had the priest come in every other day. He had come to Holy Communion. I made sure he had his Holy Communion and his last rites. Can you describe what that meant? The children. I had his grandchildren come in. I had him sneak in. And he saw them a day before Christmas. That was the last time he saw his grandchildren. I had brought them upstairs. I made them sneak in that way. Naturally, nurses would have let him in anyway. But in his condition, I just took it upon myself. Not knowing how he would take me with the shot. If he would be too great on his heart or not. But he was so excited and so happy to see him. I'm not a bit sorry now.
What about this? Can you describe the actual... Do you think you could see if you could keep them up?
Keep them up for a while. Okay? Tell them to stay out. They'll make any notes for a few minutes. Shh! Just for a few minutes, okay? Just for a few minutes.
Can you describe the actual moment of his death at that particular time? Lock the door. Yes.

I had his eyes taped down the last day. He would not close his eyes. George was a very... He was determined. He was a fighter to the very end. We had him taped down because his eyes were getting very dry. But I do remember about 20 minutes before his death, I ran downstairs to get some blood. And we had blood going in his legs and his arms. We had blood. We tried to get veins going. One had collapsed on us. We were trying to get blood going in. Because at that time, I had noticed that he was... His entire body had deteriorated. He started bleeding, hemorrhaging internally. And the doctor at that point, he was puzzled and stunned because it came on him so rapidly. And it came over in a couple hours prior to his death. We had noticed all these drastic, drastic changes. And we had given him IVs and blood and all the medications one could possibly think of in his condition. And I remember about 15 minutes before his death, I had walked out of the room and all I could think is... All I can remember is him... Running through my mind was, move the body over when he sang when he came to Columbia on a concert. Why? I don't know. That's all I could think of. And the doctor, they had warned me to step out of the room. I guess they expected it toward the end, but I was determined I wasn't going to. So about five minutes before his death, I just shook my head and I knew it was it. I started praying out loud. I was going to go. And his eyelids opened and he looked at me. And he had no feeling in his arms. His arms were so swollen, his hands were so swollen. He had paralysis in both legs at that point. He could not talk. He might give a girdle. Before this, he was gasping for breath. He had these chain stroke, stomach respirations. About five minutes before his death, he quieted down very, very, very rapidly. The breathing quieted down. We had him hooked up into an electrocardiogram that the doctor had brought in. It was his own personal electrocardiogram. The days we had that. And I was watching the machine working. It didn't look too favorable. I wasn't too happy with it. So I asked the doctor, I said, would it harm if I at least held him? I said, he looked so uncomfortable. He looked like his head was bent over. He didn't have the strength to move his head anymore. And the doctor motioned that it was all right. So I just held him in my arms for about five minutes. And I can remember him just looking up at me. And I prayed with him. And it seemed like there was just this two in the room. But there were nurses, other nurses in the room, and the doctor. They were all rushing around busily. But for some reason we both knew it was the end. Both he and I, we both knew it. And his last time was very quiet. He just took a very deep breath. And as if the evening, he just, he just, as if all the pain had just completely disappeared. And all the suffering you could just sense had gone. And there was no feeling of fighting for his life anymore. There was no more feeling of wanting to fight for his life. I mean, it was a complete, it was just complete serenity. I mean, it was like the joy that was content finally. I mean, came to the end of his road because he had mentioned to me in the hospital twice in the September visit, when he was in here with his heart attack. And then in this past visit, he said in September, when I, when I gave him this heart-of-fishing respiration, mouth-to-mouth presentation at home and brought him back, that he felt that it should have been the end then. And in the hospital, he had had a heart attack, a very serious heart attack in the middle of the night when I was with him. Before, he said to me, he says, Carolyn, I saw the gates. He said, honey, he loved it. The gates were there. And I saw them. And I wanted to walk toward him. He said, but something was preventing me from coming to him. And I said, well, do you, could you really, do you remember what it was? He said, no. He said, I didn't want to leave you behind. I didn't want to leave Shirley and the grandchildren behind. I said, well, if you feel like that again, don't fight it anymore. And I tried to console him in a religious manner. And I said, don't ever fight it anymore. He said, those gates look so inviting to me. So when he finally left, when you departed, and your Lord took him, I felt like he had seen those gates again. And this time he wasn't fighting. I just told him to keep going, not to turn back and look back and never think about anybody, but his soul and himself. So when he finally left, he was content and happy. I mean, I feel like he, at least I'm satisfied to know that he went very serenely.
At what point do you think that he knew that he was going to die?

He died January 31st. I would say... December 31st. December. I don't know why I always say January. December 31st. I'm sorry. December 31st. About two days after Christmas. And that's when we started praying heavily, both together. That's when I would try to fall asleep, and he was worried. My feet were swelling. He was so worried. He says, Carolyn, I'm going. He says, please keep your strength. You'll need it. And he tried to reassure me. I know Bill Russell, he came up and he tried to get me to sleep on a wheelchair a couple nights. He sensed that we would need that strength about two days after Christmas, because his sons came and he said, Oh, you finally made it. And he said, you finally made it. And he said, I know you're all expecting me to die. He said, I won't disappoint you this time. And he had a joking moment, even when he thought of it. He had his dentures. He was a very modest man. And he wouldn't let anybody clean his dentures or anything by myself. Or shave for that matter. I shaved him the day before Christmas. And for anybody to shave him, he wouldn't let anybody shave him. But I shaved him there in the hospital. And he took him jokingly. But I asked him if he wanted his dentures in his mouth after he was shaving. And he said, I put his uppers in. He had his head sores in his mouth. And I was trying to get them healed. And we put the dentures in. And then I asked him if I wanted to lower his nose. He said, if you do, I'll bite your finger. I mean, he still had a sense of humor. And once, before we put the tube down his nostril, I asked him, I said, is there anything you want? I said, I'll go down. Anything possibly that you may want, I'll get you. He said, get me a shot of liquor. And I said, what in the world are you going to do with a shot of liquor? He said, what would you do with it? He said, I'm going to drink it. And get drunk. He didn't have it, did he? No, no, no. No, he was just joking. Because he asked what he could have. Although, if I had known it, I would have gotten it to him. But he would have never drank it. No, he hadn't had a drink for a long time. He hadn't had a drink, oh, going on two years prior to his death. Two years, in fact, he stopped smoking a good year before his death. He wouldn't smoke. And he'd always warned me to stop smoking. You know, end up the same way he did. But as far as his illness in the hospital, he sensed it. The evening, the morning I took him in, he sensed it the evening prior to that. Because I had given him his aminopathy shots at night, Saturday night, at 10 o'clock. And that's when I had wanted to take him to the hospital. But all night, he suffered. And he had two or three during the night. I'd given him his aminopathy shots. And we weren't getting any results. His coughing had started. And every time he'd cough, he'd get to be spasmed. So we just decided best to go in. And he walked in.
You were there the night that he played his last job. Did he send at that time? I mean, did he maybe sense that that was the last time he was going to play anything? Or not?

Well, every night he played, he sensed it might be his last. But that night was extra special for one reason. I take him into his doctor's office. We had a doctor's visit that morning. Friday morning. And he had complained of a scratchy throat. And the first thing the doctor examined him, he says, Get home and get to bed. Now. And George very teasingly said, I'm working tonight. And Dr. Harmon says, Oh no, you're not. And he said, Oh yes, I am. And this went on. So when the doctor left out of the room, he says, Huh? He thinks he's going to keep me home tonight. He said, This may be my last night I'm playing and I'm going to play. I said, All right. And I said, All right. You're the boss. So the doctor must have suspected him playing that night. He went past Preservation Hall. And he said, He said, He said he saw George playing. When he asked us at the hospital whether he had played. He hadn't played. He said there was a boy that played very similar to him. He was playing at the hospital. He was playing at the hospital. So to this day the doctor has never come through. As to whether he played that Friday night or not. But when he came home, he was very, uh, he was, uh, very pleased with himself because his, uh, tone was coming back where he wanted it. His feeling was much better. He said, And the doctor thought I couldn't play. He said, I enjoyed myself immensely tonight. And he came home. He was very tired. Which he usually found, he usually was when he came home. His feet were swelling in the sun. And, uh, he says, If they asked me to play tomorrow night, I'm going to play tomorrow night too. But, uh, that Friday night, I have a, well, he's, I have a feeling he may have sensed it may be his last.
Yes, I was there at the end. He was trying to play really well. I don't know. He was.
Uh, to me, he always played well. Though we had some rough times in the beginning coming back from the hospital. A few times there. And then his, uh, planet gave him a lot of trouble ahead.

fallen or the children got hold of it. I don't know what happened but he was having an awful lot of trouble with it. And I can remember in the back room many times he'd lay there trying to fix it himself and do the repair shop and it wasn't fixed to his liking. And we'd try to fix it and cork it up and pad it up and bend the keys and so forth. And he'd run through. I do remember though the past week prior to his death, before going into the hospital, he had played many compositions he had never played in years. He was playing for me that I hadn't been familiar with. And he says, too bad that we had never gotten together to play with the musicians that they can't remember some of these tunes. And he'd run them over and somehow I couldn't even remember them now. But they were beautiful and he'd play them for me. And he'd ask me if I knew them or if I remember. It was like a guessing game.
But he played in the back? Mm-hmm. In the back. Yeah.

He played more or less for me, I think, because he knew how much I enjoyed listening to him. And he'd lie there and he'd just lie on the bed with his feet up and he'd play with his clarinet and he'd say, well, do you remember this one or do you know this one? He was quite surprised that I knew as many as I did.
Did he know, did he choose the place where he was going to be buried?

Yes. He had, when we went on All Saints, All Souls Day, I took him to the graveside and put flowers on Jeannette's grave, his wife's grave, late wife's grave, and on his mother's grave. They were both buried in the same place. And he said, this is where I'm going to be. Not here. He didn't say to me many times, I want to stop there and say some prayers. And he always said, it won't be long now before you'll be coming here. He said, because I'm going to be out here very shortly and you'll be coming to see me. Was he buried in fact, right in there with his wife and mother? In the same, in the same grave. Oh, in the same grave. Yes. You can wait a year. And I do know, I remember asking, I said, well, not having any definite place where I had buried, would I, could I possibly be buried there? And he said, yes. So my burial place is already to be in the same. Have you been out there since? Every day. I believe I missed maybe three or four days since his death. I go over there and say prayer. I told him I would never, as long as my husband, I would never stop visiting him.
But can you remember anything about this period, as I say, like the last three months of his life, where you went and stuff

a couple years, he said, but especially since September. It seemed like when he entered the hospital, it was in the latter part of September, around the 21st, if I'm not mistaken. He was in there for about eight or nine days, and I brought him home. And from then on, he seemed like he was trying to run a battle of time. He would, we rode all over the quarter. He showed me the different places where he lived. He showed me the different places where he'd go, where he used to shop, where he bought his first clarinet. And, excuse me. No, we'd go riding around. I mean, we'd go off sometimes to the doctor's office and have an early appointment, not come back until late in the afternoon. And we did want to make a trip to Manville, and we wanted to show me his home where his daddy had lived. He spoke quite a bit of his father. I remember more so than he did when I first arrived.
Yes, I'd like you to say something about that, because that's one of the things I have nothing on. He didn't ever, none of the interviews I had with him, has ever matched his father as well.

Well, he was, when Bobo was taken from me, he knew that it worried me quite a bit. And he tried to reassure me that the boys usually, regardless of what happens, they'll never forget a mother, but there's just certain feelings that they have for a father. He says he remembers since he's been a child, that when his mother and father were separated, that he would go stay with his father for the weekend. And he's so proud, he said he'd be so proud walking down the street, sometimes he'd go downtown and get a shoe shine, his dad would get a shoe shine. And he was just so proud to be one of his father. And his father, he said he was not a very, he was a quiet man. He spoke very slowly and quietly until his temper flew up. And he said there's always a few, three things that he said his daddy said, nobody would ever touch that. It was his knife he had, a pair of scissors, and his wife. And his father was not a very tall person. And he said that naturally he could never understand why his mother and daddy really separated. He always thought they'd get back together again. There was a closeness between them, but it was not the same like it had been before the separation. And he remembers his father teaching him to swim. And he remembers one time he got a really good beating, he said, after he went into the water and stayed in there all afternoon, and had a lot more of a sunstroke. And he came out and his father was very furious with him. In fact, he was so angry with him that he pleaded to come back home to his mother. And he said, no, he couldn't. He was going to stay there until his time was up, until his mother came home. And, oh, he spoke of his daddy. He went to church with him a few times. And of his one room, he had a one-room little shack, he called it, where he kept everything in his one little room. He was quite content with it.
And he said, no, I'm not going to go into it.

Mine escapes me right now. But I do know, he did mention more of his daddy in the past three months than he had spoken before. Oh, and his father enjoyed the music very much. He enjoyed traditional jazz. And he was very, very proud when he'd hear of his son playing. He always said his daddy was very proud of him when he heard of him playing, especially on the first night. His father got him the first job, I believe it was on St. Joseph's Day. And that's when he belonged to the Black Eagles. And George was just a little chaffy, I think he was about 14. And his father got that job for him. They didn't play but three tunes all night. But his father was pleased. And he said he was quite upset with his father at one point where he wanted to get a clarinet, which was very pretty in the window he had seen. And his father said, no, he was going to get a different clarinet for him, a much sturdier one that he would get more use out of. And he said the first time he handled it, he was not too pleased with it. He said because he wanted the pretty one, the shiny one. And his father got him the one he eventually got. But he said it was not the one, it was a new one. And the one he wanted was second hand.
Well, are George's clarinets still here or... Didn't Dorothy take it? What's the disposition of this?

No. One of his clarinets, the one he played, the last one he played, it's still... they're both in the back room. One Bill Russell gave him. And then there's one that he had purchased, I believe, in England. That's the one he had been playing with mostly. That was his favorite one.
Yeah. Well, that was the one he got for... That was the one I think that was supposed to be Jimmy Newman's band. Yes. Yeah.
No, I believe that... isn't that the one that Jim... Bill Russell got? Jimmy Newman's?
No, George himself got the Jimmy Newman one. Well, that's the one that he enjoys playing.

Yeah, that's the one that he was playing with. Mm-hmm. And, well, that's in the back room with his small case, and he has a double case for the two clarinets. Dorothy is taking the double case, just the case, because she got that for him. She bought it for him, and she'd like to have that. And the clarinet that Bill Russell purchased for and gave to George, and he was sending it to a Japanese boy, to... ...Woyichi Kawai. Because George always said that if anything ever happened, he would like one of his clarinets to go back to Japan. Because he loved Japan. They all treated him so royally and getting him so happy when he played there. So it hasn't been sent yet, but I'm going to give the clarinet back to Bill Russell, and Bill's going to pack it up and send it as a gift to Woyichi. The other one surely is going to hang out to. And there's one in the Smithsonian Institute now. That's the one that was, I believe, George said it was not given to the Jazz Museum, but then I hear that it was given to the Jazz Museum. That's what we sent it to us. And anyway, that was the one that has been sent up to the Smithsonian Institute. That was the one he reported to the Common Street Museum. That's right. That's when it... I believe it was given in about 1961 or 62, because that was one of my first trips. Years, I was there when they were awarded it to the Jazz Museum. Dr. Deshaun brought it in, in fact, in the newspaper. And he just says to hang out to the other one. And the piece in the middle... One thing he always said before he always went into work, not to let anybody ever get hold of it, so that I am keeping. Just for me to keep that. Which one is that? That is a piece that goes to any clarinet. The toner. Yes, I have a toner. He said, everybody's been trying to get their hands on it. He said, whatever you do, you just keep it. He says, maybe one day your son, they want to play. He says, keep it. He said, other than that... He said, nothing is more important to me than that one small piece, and that I would guard with my life and death. He says, if anybody were to grab the case, to grab that one little piece out, and actually most of the time I would carry it in my pocketbook. Why he had that certain feeling for that one special part, I do not know. But he said that was the entire... Not the layout, but the entire doing to his clarinet playing. By that. By that. My little car. In fact, I cleaned it for him one day when I arrived here. He gave it to me and I scrubbed it and I cleaned it and I didn't know what it was. That's before he told me really what it was. He let me clean his clarinet, which I was always proud of. After he cleaned it, he tried... He didn't tell me then, but I do remember one of my hospital trips that took him in. He says, Carolyn, this is out of my case, give me that one little part. He called it the tuna. That's what it was, the tuna. He says, put that in your pocketbook. He says, grab my mother's rosary beads, the tuna, and my knife, which I carry with me now. This little knife from Japan, you see. He said, those three things always take to the hospital with me. And don't ever part with any of them. Now the rosary beads I had given to Cheryl. The tuna I got, and the knife.
Did George ever talk about integration and color children?

Yes. We spoke with him quite a bit. George is a very honest person, and he was very honest and open with me especially. Naturally, both being different colors. We both knew the burden we had to face with the population and so forth. And he naturally was all for integration. He was schooled in an integrated school his early years. He couldn't understand the riots that are going on now. He says that the people were bringing it upon themselves, both races. Not one, but the other, both races. He was very frank with me. I mean, we'd joke about it because I'd always, he'd always say, he'd tan my height if I was naughty. And I'd tell him if he wasn't good, I'd tan him until he turned white. I mean, it was just a pass on joke. Yeah. Now, when he was with other people, he was very polite, very well-mannered. He wouldn't say a word. Sometimes they would hurt him in their remarks. But he was going to bite his tongue and hold back. And. And.

He was a very honest, forthright person. If he liked the person, he couldn't do enough for him. If he didn't, he would either keep clear out of the way or you would know it, one way or another. He wasn't one to, like they say, pussyfoot around. He used to hurt him so many times going to the clubs and he'd have to walk in the back way. Because I know many times after I arrived, if he played in one or two hotels or something, he said it wasn't long before this, he said I'd have to go in the back way. He said, well we've been walking together now. And if we'd walk into a restaurant to eat, it worried him somewhat. Because he was a fighter and if anybody made an unkind word in any way, he was ready. I'd sometimes have to control him rather than start something. But he says, no, nobody's going to say anything one way or another. He's got to let me know. So as far as integration goes, or the color part of it, he treated people as they treated him, regardless of color. Color was no problem to him unless they caused it. And naturally being part Indian. He had some of that Indian blood in him. He didn't like anybody talking about the Indians either because his great grandmother was Indian. So with George, as far as the color went, he loved all people of all races. If they treated him properly, he treated them. In return, I know my little, my daughter, he just loves her. I mean, he's a little guy like Mary. He said, as far as the white race went. Or Bobo. When Bobo came here. Lord, that child used to climb up on his bed all the time, hug him and kiss him and so forth. And he was so proud when I entered him into the school with David and Graham, his grandchildren. He was the first little white boy to enter that school. And he was tickle-pain. George was happy when I enrolled him in that school.
Did George, you say, what were the places he went, like Japan the best. Did he, can you say anything about that or traveling or where he likes to be out of the way and so on?

Well, Japan was his favorite. Why? I believe it was the countryside, the people themselves. He liked, he liked all traveling. He was one that, I believe, much of his illness that he had had was the fact that he couldn't travel. Toward the end, especially when his feet started getting in trouble. He liked Denmark quite a bit. He always spoke to Denmark quite highly. And Papa Boo. But everything was Japan. I don't know. He always said, he says, Carol, when I get better, he said, we're going to go back to Japan. He said, we may just stay there permanently. I mean, he just enjoyed it. He loved it. The people were nice to him. He said they treated him, a human. He put it in that type of term. And every time he left, he left part of them, he said, in Japan. He's got pictures and pictures and pictures and pictures of Japan that were taken. And I guess it's the fact that everybody idolized himself. I mean, everybody just spelled out when he came. He was treated like a king. And he loved it. He said he loved every bit of it. He said he didn't know how he would adjust to it. He adjusted quicker, more quicker than he thought he would.
Did he have any special favorites among the musicians or did he say anything about that?

Well, as far as favorites, there were no special favorites. Naturally, he liked Lawrence Moreiro. But Lawrence is gone. And he was getting a little bit displeased with the musicians toward the end because he was a perfectionist in his playing. George wanted everything to be just so. He really was a born leader when it came to a band. And it hurt him deeply when he became ill and couldn't lead, couldn't be a leader. I mean, he turned that down himself because he felt it wasn't fair to the group that since he couldn't lead, be the leader, it wouldn't give the men the opportunity to play as often. He didn't believe in all the drinking that had been going on because when he played for the public, he wanted to give his best and he wanted the musicians to do their best. Sometimes alcohol just doesn't mix. And the true playing. He didn't want to be mocked. He said he just didn't want to be mocked. He said people are coming. He said there may be, most of them are tourists, true. He said, but there are true purists that come in. And if they hear the music played in the manner it's played when the men are heavily intoxicated. He said, they allow him to make a remark. He said, and he doesn't like any remarks given out because there's no need for it. He knows the capability of some musicians that they can do had they not been in this condition. I mean, he liked Louie Nelson's playing. And he liked all the musicians playing as far as their playing goes. I'm not saying, I'm not going to say many of the remarks he made toward the end simply because I have a feeling that he didn't mean some of it that he had said.
Yeah, well, it's just better not playing again.

Yeah, that he himself was having trouble. But George was a perfectionist in this playing. I mean, he was beautiful. When he played, he wanted to give himself completely. He got lost in this playing. Like I always used to say, whenever I thought of George Lewis's playing, or now for that matter, I would always tease him and I'd say, well, tonight you're going to go play with the angels again. Because to me, that's how he sounded, like he was talking to the angels when he played. Just talking with those angels. And he felt it because he said his mom always told him. She said, son, when you get up on that stage, when you're playing, don't ever say, I'm playing this for George Lewis. He says, I'm playing this for Jesus. Always say, I'm playing this for you, Jesus. And there was always that. He said, never once did he ever stop, did he ever get to play in front of the public, where he didn't say that to him, son. Or if he came back on tour, his mother always, she'd say, he'd come in the door and he would say, his mama would say, well, son, how did you make out? How did you all make out? And he says, oh, ma, I made out pretty good. She says, look, I didn't ask you, son, how you made out. She says, I asked you how you all made out. She says, because it didn't take just but you to play that group, to go overseas and play for the people. She said, it took the entire group. When you're speaking, she says, you're speaking of the group. And he said, they never forgot it. So when he spoke of his playing, he never spoke really. That's why he was so unhappy with the group if they didn't play up to his standard of what he wants to at all times, because he felt he himself wasn't playing. It was an entire group. It was just not singular. And he said, each man had to give of himself. They all contributed.

And he said, I don't know. Do you remember anything else about the last, say that last three month period or anything that's particularly memorable or anything in conclusion that the 73 sisters would like to say about George or remembering anything you remember especially?

Oh, not really, Tom. All I can think of is that he's the most wonderful person I've ever met. I mean, his playing to me naturally will always be the greatest thing. He's always been my idol since I've been a child. And for me to come in contact, as I had with him, with an idol, which was like some teenagers go after movie stars, he was mine. And then to know him as I had with him. And then to know him as I had known him. It's just like a dream come true. I mean, it's a dream come true and now it's a dream, just a dream. But his playing will always be beautiful to me. His playing will always be talking with the angels. And that's what he's doing at the moment. He always said not to, he always said, the musicians now, the young ones, that he was hoping that there would be more younger ones following in the traditional vein. Which, it didn't please him to know that there weren't too many followers. Like Shirley had mentioned, he didn't disapprove of any musical full on. He didn't approve of all of it, but he didn't disapprove of it either. But he was saddened to know that there weren't more younger groups playing in the same vein in his race. And he said it took a long time for the people now in his race to realize the artistry in it, from what it had been. It's just recent. And as far as anything about George Lewis, George Lewis was a great person, a great man. Well, I think we better stop this. Yeah. Now Shirley, I'm going to wait to share.

segments.title: Entering the hospital on December 15 and the salt-free diet
segments.summary: Carolyn Buck describes taking George Lewis to hospital with asthma and a sore throat, the doctors Hyman, the tent, the Hong Kong flu and his loss of appetite on a salt-free diet.

segments.title: His premonition, wishes for his music, and prayer in the hospital
segments.summary: He told her he would not come home for Christmas, spoke of grandchildren, Shirley and his music, planned his funeral music, and they prayed with his mother's rosary and crucifix.

segments.title: The afternoon before he died: the crucifix and his last words
segments.summary: She fetches his mother's crucifix, puts it in his hand at 11 p.m.; he dies at 2:15 and his last words were that he would come back for her. He asks for happy funeral music and a church service despite being a Mason.

segments.title: Last wishes: Japan, his clothing, no hasty decisions
segments.summary: He wanted to tour again and return to Japan, and asked that his belongings not be dealt with too hastily. Recording interruptions.

segments.title: Visitors in the hospital: Dorothy Tate, Bill Russell, sons, priest, grandchildren
segments.summary: Dorothy Tate, Bill Russell (a 'living saint'), Louis Nelson and his sons visit; the priest gives communion and last rites; she smuggles the grandchildren in the day before Christmas.

segments.title: The moment of his death
segments.summary: Interruption to keep the children quiet, then a detailed account of his final hours, internal bleeding, her holding him, and his serene passing, with his earlier vision of the gates.

segments.title: When he knew he was dying; his humor and habits
segments.summary: He said he was going after Christmas, joked with his sons and about a shot of liquor, and had given up drinking and smoking; she recounts the night before admission.

segments.title: His last job at Preservation Hall and the doctor's warning
segments.summary: Against the doctor's orders he played his last Friday night, pleased his tone was returning; the interviewer recalls his playing near the end.

segments.title: Playing old tunes for her at home on his troubled clarinet
segments.summary: In his final week he played long-forgotten compositions for her in the back room while struggling with clarinet repairs.

segments.title: Choosing his burial place with his wife and mother
segments.summary: They visited the graves on All Saints Day; he would be buried in the same grave as his late wife Jeannette and his mother, and she visits daily.

segments.title: Riding through the French Quarter in his last three months
segments.summary: After a September hospital stay he showed her where he had lived, shopped and bought his first clarinet, and spoke more about his father.

segments.title: His father: childhood memories and getting his first job
segments.summary: Lewis recalled weekends with his father after his parents separated, his father's character, learning to swim, and his father getting him a first job with the Black Eagles at about 14 and choosing his clarinet.

segments.title: What became of his clarinets and the special piece he kept
segments.summary: Discussion of his surviving clarinets, one Bill Russell gave him, the Smithsonian and Jazz Museum, the one going to Japan, and a small clarinet part she keeps along with rosary and knife.

segments.title: His views on integration and race
segments.summary: She discusses their mixed marriage, his support for integration, his reaction to riots, his having to enter clubs by the back way, and his Indian ancestry.

segments.title: Japan and Denmark as his favorite places to travel
segments.summary: He loved Japan above all, for its countryside and the way people treated him like a king, and also spoke highly of Denmark.

segments.title: His standards for the band and objections to drinking
segments.summary: Lewis liked Lawrence Marrero and Louis Nelson, was a perfectionist and born leader, gave up leading when ill, and disliked musicians playing drunk.

segments.title: Playing for Jesus and for the whole group, as his mother taught him
segments.summary: His mother told him to dedicate his playing to Jesus and to speak of how the whole group played, which shaped his unhappiness when the band fell short.

segments.title: Closing remembrances: idol, angels and the future of traditional jazz
segments.summary: She calls him the most wonderful person she met, his playing like talking with angels, and says he wished more young players followed traditional jazz.
